synopsis: The corpus treats image and field similarity as measures of appearance and structure, not proof of perception or safety equivalence: PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS require pixel-matched pairs, whereas FID compares image collections [f14791, f14773, f14771]. Chapter 5 documents substantial viewpoint sensitivity: Para-Lane (2025) falls from 22.99 dB PSNR in the recorded lane to 17.05 dB in the adjacent lane, while MV² (August 2026) falls from 29.13 dB at drone height to 10.36 dB from a car; these results are on-road evidence [f3707, f3709]. Generative novel-view methods achieved 13.19–20.82 dB PSNR on Waymo in a 2026 preprint, which the booklet interprets as low fidelity for safety testing rather than metric-faithful validation [f3821, f3822, f4330]. Across Chapters 6 and 9, improved visual or radar-map similarity does not reliably imply equivalent system behavior: RadaRays improved mutual-information and structural-similarity scores, yet a detector trained on real radar images still failed on simulated images [f4824, f14776, f7071]. Whether FID and certain geometric distances predict safety-relevant perception errors remains uncertain, and FID does not target a specific perception algorithm [f5067, f4819]. Planning should therefore pair image similarity with task-level and closed-loop validation, checking higher assessment layers rather than inferring them from lower-layer agreement [f4827, f14778, f14797].
